citation.authors: Cressman EK, Salomonczyk D, Henriques DYP
citation.title: Visuomotor adaptation and proprioceptive recalibration in older adults

study.eligibility_rationale: All four criteria hold. (1) Upper-extremity visuomotor rotation task: "the cursor representing the hand position was gradually rotated 30 CW with respect to the hand over the first 41 trials in increments of 0.75". (2) Older vs younger samples: "Nine healthy older subjects between the ages of 61 and 80 ... and ten healthy young subjects between the ages of 18 and 36". (3) Both perturbation-block reaching and no-cursor (perturbation/feedback removed) reaching reported: "Fig. 3 Visuomotor adaptation during the a reach training trials and b aftereffect trials". (4) Written in English.
study.design_notes: Single experiment, within-subject two-day design: day 1 = aligned-cursor baseline (reach training, no-cursor reaches, proprioceptive estimates), day 2 = same tasks with the cursor gradually rotated 30° CW. The rotated day is the participants' first (and only) exposure to the distortion, so the age contrast on day 2 is a first-exposure contrast; the aligned day serves as the baseline that is subtracted for the aftereffect ("average deviations for trials completed after reaching with an aligned cursor were then subtracted from average deviations after reaching with a rotated cursor"). No cursor reaches were collected twice on each day (12 trials after reach training, 15 trials at the end); the authors report the FIRST set for the extent of adaptation because "we found no difference in reaches completed before and after the Proprioceptive Estimate + Reach Task". Note a small context change in the final no-cursor set only ("all 5 reach targets and reference marker positions were now presented") — that set is not the one used for the aftereffect measure. Reach training used 4 targets (5° and 30° left and right of centre); proprioceptive estimation used 3 reference markers and is a separate, non-protocol outcome. Ns are consistent between Methods and the analyses (degrees of freedom of 17 for between-group tests, t(9) young / t(8) older). Reach-training data are plotted as 33 blocks of three trials (Fig. 3a); no numeric table of block values is printed.

outcomes.measure_name: Mean angular deviation of the hand at peak velocity while reaching with the misaligned (30° CW rotated) cursor
outcomes.higher_is_better_evidence: However, hand deviations did increase over blocks of trials as expected with the increased distortion in order to guide the rotated cursor to the target in a more direct path (F(32, 544) = 45.261, P\0.001).
outcomes.operationalization: Hand deviation at peak velocity (angular difference between the home-target reference vector and the home-hand vector at PV) during the 99 reach-training trials completed with the gradually introduced 30° CW rotated cursor; deviations averaged over 3 consecutive trials giving 33 blocks per subject (Fig. 3a, misaligned/squares). Late adaptation corresponds to the final block(s) of this series (the text states saturation occurred by Block 13 in young and from Block 10 in older subjects). No numeric block means are printed in the text; only the figure plots them.

outcomes.measure_ruling: measure: baseline_corrected. winner: In b, we show mean hand deviations on aftereffect trials averaged across subjects and targets. Results are shown in degrees and as a percentage of the distortion introduced during reach training trials. Aftereffects are presented taking performance on reaches completed after reaching with an aligned cursor as baseline, such that hand deviations achieved on the no cursor reaching trials after reaching with an aligned cursor were subtracted from corresponding hand deviations achieved after reaching with a misaligned cursor. | loser: On average, subjects recalibrated proprioception by 20% and adapted their reaches by 60% of the visual distortion introduced. | The protocol asks for performance after removal of the perturbation and feedback, in the post-learning phase immediately following the initial perturbation block, using the block average when reported. That is exactly what Fig. 3b plots: the group-mean hand deviation at peak velocity on the first set of no-cursor reaches, averaged across trials and targets and expressed relative to the aligned-cursor baseline ("The extent of visuomotor adaptation was examined by looking at the angular deviations of the hand in the first set of no cursor reaches"; "Hand deviations were averaged across all 12 trials for each subject and the average deviations for trials completed after reaching with an aligned cursor were then subtracted from average deviations after reaching with a rotated cursor", p6). Fig. 3b's degree axis and percent axis are the SAME pair of bars read against two axes, i.e. one measure written twice, so both expressions of those marks remain readable; the winning measure is named as the baseline-corrected group-mean aftereffect. The other percentage expressions are separate candidate measures and lose: the p8 "60%" figure is pooled across both age groups ("On average, subjects") and therefore carries no group-specific value, and Fig. 5's x axis plots only individual subject points with no group summary ("The changes in proprioceptive estimates are plotted as a function of changes in reach aftereffects for each subject", p9).

datasets.notes: Late adaptation: hand deviation at peak velocity late in the 99-trial rotated reach-training block, Fig. 3a (33 blocks of 3 trials); text reports group statistics only ("RM-ANOVA revealed no differences between the two groups with respect to hand deviations achieved across the blocks of learning trials (Group: F(1, 17) = 2.523, P = 0.131..."). Aftereffect: no-cursor reaches, Fig. 3b, reported as misaligned-minus-aligned difference ("On average, all subjects reached 18.0 more left of the target following reach training with a misaligned cursor"; "no differences between the two age groups with respect to the extent of visuomotor adaptation achieved (t(17) < 1)"). Group-specific means/SDs for these two outcomes are shown only graphically in Fig. 3.
